content: If a healthcare provider is reasonably certain that a woman is not pregnant, an intrauterine device (IUD) can be safely inserted. Pregnancies that occur in women using IUDs are associated with an increased risk of complications, including spontaneous abortion, septic abortion, preterm delivery, and chorioamnionitis. A systematic review evaluated the diagnostic accuracy of a pregnancy checklist compared to a concurrent urine pregnancy test. The sensitivity of the checklist ranged from 55% to 100%, while specificity ranged from 39% to 89%. However, the negative predictive value was consistently high at 99% to 100%, indicating that the checklist reliably ruled out pregnancy in women who were not pregnant. One study assessed the additional value of including signs and symptoms of pregnancy in the checklist but found that these criteria did not significantly improve its performance. The number of women with such signs and symptoms in the study was small. Fewer than 1 in 100 women become pregnant during the first year of IUD use with typical use. IUDs are long-acting, reversible contraceptive methods that can be used by women of all ages, including adolescents, and by both parous and nulliparous women. However, IUDs do not provide protection against sexually transmitted diseases (STDs). Consistent and correct use of male latex condoms is recommended to reduce the risk of STDs, including HIV. The copper IUD (Cu-IUD) can be inserted at any time if it is reasonably certain that the woman is not pregnant. It can also be used as emergency contraception if inserted within 5 days of unprotected sexual intercourse. If the day of ovulation can be estimated, the Cu-IUD may be inserted more than 5 days after intercourse, provided it is not inserted more than 5 days after ovulation. No additional contraceptive protection is needed after Cu-IUD insertion. For women with amenorrhea (not postpartum), the Cu-IUD can be inserted at any time if pregnancy can be reasonably excluded. No backup contraception is required in this case. Similarly, when switching from another contraceptive method, the Cu-IUD can be inserted immediately without waiting for the next menstrual period, provided pregnancy is reasonably excluded. No additional contraceptive protection is needed in this scenario. If a healthcare provider cannot be reasonably certain that a woman is not pregnant, an alternative contraceptive method should be provided until pregnancy can be ruled out, at which point the Cu-IUD can be inserted. Evidence suggests that the timing of Cu-IUD insertion in relation to the menstrual cycle in non-postpartum women has little effect on long-term outcomes, such as continuation rates, removal rates, expulsion rates, or pregnancy rates, as well as short-term outcomes like pain or bleeding at insertion. The levonorgestrel-releasing IUD (LNG-IUD) can also be inserted at any time if it is reasonably certain that the woman is not pregnant. If the LNG-IUD is inserted within the first 7 days of menstrual bleeding, no additional contraceptive protection is required.
